metadata.title: How to Argue Without Cheating.
metadata.purpose: Six cards. Two about how you show up to an argument. Four about moves that break one. The source carousel embedded a contested political conclusion inside a civility rule — which is the fallacy the film exists to name. The rewrites remove the premise without discarding the teaching. The bidirectional examples are not balance: they are the actual test of whether you have learned the tool or just a new way to dismiss your opponents.
metadata.source: Six-card social-media carousel on argumentation fallacies and conduct. Two conduct cards (LISTEN, BE RESPECTFUL) and four fallacy cards (RED HERRING, ANECDOTAL EVIDENCE, AD HOMINEM, FALSE DILEMMA). Card grammar kept. Design rebuilt in Claude tokens — source charcoal/white/red is another creator's visual identity. Three cards rewritten: BE RESPECTFUL → GOOD FAITH (source embedded a contested political premise); ANECDOTAL EVIDENCE sharpened to preserve the legitimate counterexample use; AD HOMINEM narrowed to distinguish the fallacy from source-reliability assessment. All deviations documented in FACTCHECK.md.
metadata.color_semantics: TERRACOTTA = the accent. On fallacy cards: icon strokes. On conduct cards: the test/rule line. One moment per card.

beats.narration_text: Bonjour — this is Liam, in for Bear. Here is a question worth sitting with. How do you tell a bad argument from an argument you happen to dislike? Because the answer is not obvious, and the gap between them is where most arguments go to die.

props.command: How do I tell a bad argument from an argument I dislike?
output: You can catch yourself running them.
Six tools. Two rules. Zero excuses.

beats.narration_text: Six cards. Two are about how you show up to an argument — conduct. Four are about moves that break the structure of an argument — fallacies. These are not partisan tools. They work on everyone who uses them, including you.

lines: Two on how you show up.
Four on moves that break arguments.

beats.narration_text: Card one: LISTEN. Not wait. Waiting for someone to finish is not listening. Listening means you can state their position in a form they would accept. If you cannot do that, you have not heard it yet. The test is simple and uncomfortable: before you respond, say back what you heard. Not your interpretation. Their position.

props.title: LISTEN
props.definition: Waiting for someone to finish is not listening.
props.test: Can you state their position in a form they would accept? If not, you have not heard it yet.

beats.narration_text: Card two: GOOD FAITH. Assume the other person is arguing in good faith until they show you otherwise. Grace is cheap. It also keeps the exchange alive long enough to get somewhere. The alternative — assuming bad faith from the start — guarantees the conversation produces only heat.

props.title: GOOD FAITH
props.definition: Assume the other person is arguing in good faith until they show you otherwise.
props.test: Grace is cheap. It also keeps the exchange alive long enough to get somewhere.

beats.narration_text: Card three: RED HERRING. Answering an argument by raising a different issue. The test: does the reply engage the thing that was actually said? A claim about a specific policy answered with a claim about a different group's conduct. A claim about conduct answered with a procedural objection. Neither of those is an answer.

props.title: RED HERRING
props.definition: Answering an argument by raising a different issue.
examples: A policy claim answered with a different group's conduct.
A conduct claim answered with a procedural objection.
props.test: Does the reply engage the thing that was actually said?

beats.narration_text: The test: what kind of claim is being made? If the claim is universal — always, never, impossible — one case is enough to break it. If the claim is probabilistic — common, rare, more likely — one case cannot touch it. The anecdote is doing the right job in the first situation and the wrong job in the second.

lines: Universal claim: one case breaks it.
Rate claim: one case cannot touch it.
The anecdote only knows which kind you made.

beats.narration_text: Card five: AD HOMINEM. Attacking the arguer instead of the argument. Latin: against the man. The test: would the argument still stand if a different person made it? If yes, the attack was not an answer. Telling someone they are not qualified, so their reading of the study is worthless — that is not a refutation. The study says what it says regardless of who cites it.

props.title: AD HOMINEM
props.definition: Attacking the arguer instead of the argument. Latin: against the man.
examples: "You are not qualified, so your reading of the study is worthless."
Any insult offered in place of a reason.
props.test: Would the argument still stand if a different person made it? If yes, the attack was not an answer.

beats.narration_text: Card six: FALSE DILEMMA. Two options presented as if they were the only two. Either we ship Friday or the quarter is lost. Either you support this policy or you want harm for this group. The test: name a third option. If one exists, the fork was built, not found. And in most real arguments, several more options exist.

props.title: FALSE DILEMMA
props.definition: Two options presented as if they were the only two.
examples: "Either we ship Friday or the quarter is lost."
A contested question reduced to being for one group or against another.
props.test: Name a third option. If one exists, the fork was built, not found.

beats.narration_text: The test of whether you understand a fallacy is whether you can catch yourself running it. Not theirs. Yours. Six cards. Two on conduct: listen, and extend good faith. Four on structure: the herring, the anecdote, the attack on the person, the false fork. All six work the same way in every direction.

artifactLines: LISTEN — can you state their case in their own words?
GOOD FAITH — assume it until shown otherwise.
AD HOMINEM — the arguer is not the argument.
FALSE DILEMMA — name the third option.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: 'Here is an argument I recently made. Paste it here. Identify any moves that substitute a feeling about the speaker or the situation for an actual reason. What would a steel-manned version of the opposing position look like?' Run it on something you argued — not something you heard from the other side. What comes back may be uncomfortable. That is the point. Liam, in for Bear.

props.command: Identify moves that substitute a feeling for a reason. Steel-man the opposing position.
output: Run this on something you argued.
Not something you heard from the other side.
